children: Jefferies sees steady credit demand and contained credit costs, but higher rates could put pressure on funding costs and margins

Non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) are seeing healthy loan demand and resilient asset quality in the September quarter so far, although a potential rise in interest rates could increase their funding costs, according to a Jefferies report.

The report, based on discussions with nine NBFCs at the Jefferies India Forum 2026, said demand remained strong across vehicle finance, consumer lending, micro, small and medium enterprise (MSME) loans and other segments. Early festive-season trends have also been encouraging, although the timing of major festivals could influence September-quarter performance.
Jefferies said most NBFCs reported strong second-quarter growth trends, with asset quality remaining stable despite September typically being a seasonally weaker quarter.

The brokerage expects most NBFCs to maintain broadly range-bound net interest margins (NIMs) in financial year 2026-27. While higher policy rates could increase the cost of funds with a lag, lenders could partly offset the impact through loan repricing and changes in their lending mix.

Shriram Finance expects assets under management to grow about 17 per cent in FY27 and 18-20 per cent in FY28-29. Aditya Birla Capital expects an annualised growth rate of 25 per cent between FY26 and FY29.
Rate Hikes Could Raise Funding Costs
The impact of higher interest rates is expected to vary across lenders depending on their borrowing structures and loan books.

NBFCs with a larger share of floating-rate loans could reprice their assets and cushion some of the increase in funding costs. However, lenders with a higher proportion of fixed-rate loans could face greater pressure on margins if borrowing costs rise.

A separate analysis of the sector noted that yields on government securities, corporate bonds and NBFC borrowings have already increased since June, while bank lending to NBFCs has also expanded sharply.

For now, Jefferies expects NIMs to remain broadly stable in the near term. Sustained credit demand, asset-quality trends and the pace of any change in interest rates will remain key factors for NBFC performance through FY27.
